source_text: Definis hominem, si de fornicatione nascatur, reum non esse; si de coniugio, innocentem non esse. Huc enim pervenit quod dixisti bonum naturale de adulteriis posse subsistere, malum originale etiam de coniugio trahi
pass_a_gloss: You define a human being, if he is born from fornication, not to be guilty; if from marriage, not to be innocent. For to this has come what you said, that a natural good can subsist even from adulteries, but original evil is drawn even from marriage.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: You declare a human being guiltless if born from fornication, but not innocent if born from marriage. That is where your statement leads: a natural good can arise from adultery, while original evil is derived even from marriage.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Keep Julian's good-of-nature vs good-of-will contrast; do not baptize as 'grace'.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, De nuptiis et concupiscentia 2 / On Marriage and Concupiscence); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
